interest: This file offers a valuable window into the complex legal and diplomatic realities of property ownership between the United States and Japan during the 1930s. It illuminates the winding down of the Meiji-era perpetual leasehold system in former treaty ports, illustrating how Western powers negotiated the transition of extraterritorial-style property privileges into standard Japanese fee simple ownership and municipal taxation. Crucially, the records reveal how discriminatory U.S. state-level Alien Land Laws (such as those in Idaho and Washington) interacted with international treaties and Japanese reciprocity statutes, showing how state laws restricting Japanese land tenure prompted legal scrutiny of American rights in Japan. Additionally, the file provides rare documentation of American expatriate property ownership in pre-WWII Japan, from prominent cultural figures like modernist architect Antonin Raymond in Tokyo to missionary estates in Karuizawa and emerging labor and anti-Japanese boycotts in pre-war Hawaii.
overview: State Department decimal file 894.5211 covers the period from October 1931 to October 1939 and documents legal, diplomatic, and practical questions surrounding the rights of United States nationals to hold, acquire, inherit, and lease real property in Japan, as well as reciprocal restrictions under U.S. state alien land laws. Major subjects include British diplomatic initiatives in 1931 to terminate perpetual leaseholdings held by foreigners in Japanese treaty ports in exchange for government bonds and fee simple title; legal inquiries from American executors and attorneys regarding probate procedures, succession duties, and the devise of real estate in Japan (such as missionary properties in Karuizawa and estates in Yokohama and Nara); State Department analyses of the Japanese Civil Code, the Japanese Alien Land Law of 1925, and bilateral treaties of commerce and navigation (1894 and 1911); lists of American citizens known to own land in fee simple in Japan; state-level alien land law inquiries from Georgia, Idaho, and Washington concerning whether treaties granted reciprocal ownership or leasing rights to Japanese subjects; and union protests in Hawaii against commercial land acquisitions by Japanese enterprises.

subfiles.about: Cross-references Despatch No. 348 regarding negotiations to wind up foreign perpetual leaseholds in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet recording that Despatch No. 348 dated October 9, 1931, from Edwin L. Neville in Japan, has been indexed and filed under decimal number 894.52/36. The underlying paper addresses whether American nationals in Japan should cooperate with British subjects in negotiations to liquidate foreign perpetual leaseholds.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 348 on Perpetual Leases

subfiles.about: Reports on British diplomatic initiatives to terminate perpetual leases held by foreigners in Japan and requests Department instructions.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville reports that the British Ambassador to Japan is initiating negotiations with Japanese authorities and leaseholders to wind up perpetual lease holdings by British subjects. Under the proposed plan, leaseholders would calculate the tax differential between perpetual lease ground rent and fee simple property taxes, capitalized on an agreed basis for five percent Japanese government bonds, in exchange for title deeds in fee simple and equal taxation. Neville notes that American leaseholders have approached him seeking to participate with the British leaseholders' committee and recommends informal Embassy cooperation while requesting instructions from Washington.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 348 from Edwin L. Neville on Liquidation of Foreign Perpetual Leaseholds

subfiles.about: Inquires regarding Japanese legal requirements for effectuating the devise of real property in Karuizawa under an American will.
subfiles.from: Isaac A. Pennypacker (Pepper, Bodine, Stokes & Schoch, Philadelphia)
subfiles.summary: Attorney Isaac A. Pennypacker writes on behalf of the Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company, executor of the estate of Jane L. Correll, concerning land and buildings situated in Karuizawa, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. The real estate was inherited from her late husband, Reverend Irvin H. Correll, an Episcopal missionary in Japan, and devised under her Pennsylvania will to their daughter, Florence C. Newell. Pennypacker asks the Department of State for information on Japanese legal requirements for effectuating a devise of real estate under a foreign will probated at the testatrix's domicile.
subfiles.title: Letter from Isaac A. Pennypacker on Devise of Karuizawa Real Estate Under Correll Will

subfiles.about: Declines to express an official opinion on foreign law and refers the inquirer to private law firms specializing in Japanese law.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, for the Acting Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Pennypacker's inquiry regarding Japanese legal requirements for devising real estate under a foreign will. He explains that it is the State Department's established policy to refrain from rendering opinions on the provisions of foreign law and that the Department cannot comply with the request. Hornbeck suggests that information may be obtained from specialized attorneys in New York, specifically McIvor, Kauffman, Smith & Yamamoto and Alexander Tison, while disclaiming official responsibility for their standing.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Isaac A. Pennypacker Regarding Japanese Real Estate Law

subfiles.about: Apologizes to Isaac A. Pennypacker for the delay in answering his inquiry caused by a misplaced departmental file.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: A supplementary letter addressed to Isaac A. Pennypacker regarding the Department's formal reply of the same date. The author expresses regret that an administrative delay in answering the inquiry of December 14, 1933, resulted from the temporary misplacement of the file within the State Department.
subfiles.title: Letter of Apology from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Isaac A. Pennypacker for Misplaced File

subfiles.about: Inquires whether American citizens in Japan may convey property by will and asks about Japanese probate, taxes, and treaties.
subfiles.from: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)
subfiles.summary: John B. Wilson, Secretary of State of Georgia, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull following citizen inquiries regarding property rights in Japan. He requests information on whether American citizens residing in Japan may convey title to real and personal property by will, how probate is handled under Japanese law, and whether Japanese inheritance taxes apply to property in Japan or in the United States. He also asks for copies of any relevant bilateral treaties between the United States and Japan dealing with these questions.
subfiles.title: Letter from John B. Wilson (Georgia Secretary of State) on Property and Inheritance Laws in Japan
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull (Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.)

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum analyzing Japanese statutory law and court practice governing the administration of foreign estates and wills.
subfiles.from: E. H. D. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: An internal memorandum analyzing Japanese legal practice regarding the settlement of estates of deceased foreigners. The author notes that Japanese law directs that the national law of the deceased applies and that Japanese courts almost invariably exercise jurisdiction when real property in Japan is involved. The memorandum contrasts court practices in foreign settlements like Yokohama, where foreign wills are readily proved, with provincial courts (citing the case of Irene Mann in Nara around 1916-1917), which often decline jurisdiction unless real property is situated in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Estate Settlement Practices in Japan
subfiles.to: Mr. Ward and Mr. Turner (Department of State)

subfiles.about: Provides comprehensive information and legal excerpts on Japanese probate procedure, alien land laws, and treaty tax provisions.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State R. Walton Moore sends a detailed informational reply to the Secretary of State of Georgia answering questions regarding Japanese probate and property law. Quoting published legal digests by J. E. de Becker and Dr. Rokuichiro Masujima, the letter explains that succession and wills of foreigners are governed by their home national and state laws, and succession taxes apply only to property situated in Japan. Moore notes that Article I of the Japanese Alien Land Law of 1925 allows reciprocal restrictions against citizens of countries or states limiting Japanese land rights, but that it has not been invoked against Americans, and cites Article I of the 1894 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation ensuring non-discriminatory taxation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Assistant Secretary R. Walton Moore to John B. Wilson on Japanese Estate and Land Laws
subfiles.to: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)

subfiles.about: Preliminary acknowledgement of Georgia's inquiry on Japanese property rights promising a substantive study and response.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: An interim acknowledgement from Assistant Secretary of State R. Walton Moore to Georgia Secretary of State John B. Wilson regarding his letter of August 19, 1936. The letter states that the Department lacks authoritative information immediately on hand regarding Japanese property and inheritance laws. It promises that a study of available materials will be undertaken and a substantive reply provided in the near future.
subfiles.title: Preliminary Acknowledgement from R. Walton Moore to John B. Wilson
subfiles.to: John B. Wilson (Secretary of State of Georgia, Atlanta)

subfiles.about: Identifies American citizens known through diplomatic residence to own land in fee simple in Japan.
subfiles.from: J. W. B. and W. T. T. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: An internal memorandum noting that the Department of State maintains no official register of American citizens holding land in fee simple in Japan and would require consular inquiries to compile an authoritative list. Drawing on long personal residence in Japan, the officers identify four Americans known to own real property: R. M. Andrews in Tokyo, Alfred R. Child in Kamakura, architect Antonin Raymond in Tokyo, and Sigmund Isaacs in Yokohama. The memorandum notes that while many other Americans hold real rights such as leases or superficies, fee simple ownership is less certain.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on American Citizens Owning Land in Fee Simple in Japan

subfiles.about: Inquires whether any treaty permits U.S. citizens to own real estate in Japan to satisfy reciprocity under Idaho's alien land law.
subfiles.from: William H. Witty (Attorney at Law, Pocatello, Idaho)
subfiles.summary: Attorney William H. Witty of Pocatello, Idaho, writes to the Department of State on behalf of an alien Japanese client who acquired title to real estate in Idaho. Witty explains that Idaho state statutes prohibit ineligible aliens from holding title to real property unless authorized by a treaty between the United States and the alien's home country. He requests immediate advice and copies of any treaty still in force permitting American citizens to own real estate in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from William H. Witty Inquiring on Treaty Rights for Japanese Land Ownership in Idaho

subfiles.about: Reviews the 1923 Idaho alien land statute and its strict requirement of an authorizing treaty for land tenure by ineligible aliens.
subfiles.summary: Treaty Division official J. T. Keating reports to Division Chief Charles M. Barnes on his examination of the Idaho statutes regarding alien land ownership. He notes that under the Idaho statute of 1923, Section 2, aliens ineligible for U.S. citizenship may own real property only where explicitly provided by treaty. Keating advises that because Idaho law requires a treaty rather than statutory reciprocity, the Department need not mention Japanese domestic statutes that might provide for reciprocal ownership.
subfiles.title: Internal Memorandum by J. T. Keating on Idaho Alien Land Statute

subfiles.about: Informs William H. Witty that no treaty in force permits U.S. citizens to own real property in Japan, citing the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.from: Charles M. Barnes (Chief, Treaty Division, for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Charles M. Barnes, Chief of the Treaty Division, replies to William H. Witty's inquiry regarding treaty rights to own real estate. He advises that there is no treaty in force between the United States and Japan permitting American citizens to own real property in Japan. Barnes explains that while Article I of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation governs property interests that nationals may acquire, those interests do not encompass fee simple ownership of real estate, and encloses a copy of the treaty.
subfiles.title: Letter from Charles M. Barnes to William H. Witty on Treaty Provisions and Real Estate Ownership

subfiles.about: Inquires by telegram whether the 1911 treaty clause on commercial and residential leasing is in force and whether time limitations exist.
subfiles.summary: The law firm of Cherry and Hull in Yakima, Washington, sends a telegraphic inquiry to the Secretary of State regarding the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. They request immediate confirmation whether the treaty provision granting citizens of both nations liberty to lease land for residential and commercial purposes is currently in force. They also ask whether the treaty establishes any specific limitation on how long commercial leases may run.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Cherry and Hull Inquiring on Treaty Leasing Provisions and Commercial Lease Limits

subfiles.about: Telegraphs Cherry and Hull confirming that Article I of the 1911 treaty is in force and contains no specific term limits on commercial leases.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull replies by telegram to Cherry and Hull confirming that Article I of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation remains in force. He states that the treaty contains no specific limitations regarding the duration of commercial leases. Hull highlights the treaty clause providing that leases must be held upon the same terms as native citizens or subjects, subject to established local laws and regulations.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Cordell Hull to Cherry and Hull Clarifying Commercial Lease Terms Under 1911 Treaty

subfiles.about: Cross-references a labor protest against the establishment and property acquisition of a Mitsukoshi department store in Honolulu.
subfiles.from: Metal Trades Council of Hawaii (via Department of Labor)
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet referencing an October 25, 1939 letter transferred from the Department of Labor, filed under decimal file 611a.9417/1. The document concerns a formal protest by the Metal Trades Council of Hawaii against the establishment of a Honolulu branch of the Mitsukoshi Department Store. The union objected to Japanese aliens purchasing property in the United States solely to sell Japanese-manufactured goods and hire exclusively Japanese personnel.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Protest Against Mitsukoshi Department Store in Honolulu
subfiles.to: Department of State / Department of Labor
